It sets itself apart from naive subsampling by ensuring that the expected value of the estimated loss and its gradients match those of the full dense objective, allowing stochastic optimization to converge to the same optimum while significantly reducing computational cost [S1].

The claim states that the method sets itself apart from naive subsampling by ensuring the expected value of the estimated loss and its gradients match those of the full dense objective, allowing convergence to the same optimum while reducing computational cost. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'By incorporating appropriate importance weights... the Monte Carlo estimator produces an unbiased estimate of the dense loss. Consequently, the expected value of the estimated loss and its gradients match those of the dense loss, allowing stochastic optimization to converge to the same optimum while significantly reducing computational cost.' It further contrasts this with naive subsampling, noting that 'A naive subsampling from a non-uniform distribution leads to a biased estimator... To correct this, we use importance-weighted Monte Carlo estimation.' The mathematical proofs in the source confirm $E[L_{MC}] = L_{dense}$ and $E[grad_{MC}] = grad_{dense}$. Therefore, every fact in the claim is supported by the evidence.
